persons.name: David Curtin
persons.note: THE LADDER'S OWN READING OF THIS EVIDENCE. Read from poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1c), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1834 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Curtin, David” (poll_1834_029, line 198). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Curtin' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

persons.name: Wm. Osborn
persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Osbern, Wm.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Osborn, William, | 1834, May 1, | Ridgefield, Conn. | 67 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'william' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json).

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD — no trade recorded, in the south division, where it is counted after the re-family recorded above; it was drawn in the west division. NOBODY HERE IS NAMED BY ANY SOURCE. The 1840 Chicago schedule counts children under ten at 27% of the town and women of twenty to twenty-nine as its second-largest band; the 1835 layer the sources can name holds 15 women, because the rolls that name this town — a letter list, a voters' roll, a subscription — print men. That gap is the shape of the evidence and not a reading of the town, so the order book counts it bucket by bucket and this household is drawn against those counts. Every value on it carries the model row and the seed that redraws it, and a source naming a woman who kept her own house in this division retires the whole record. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). This household is one of the surplus the re-cut HOLDS rather than retires: the owner's ruling of 2026-09-24 re-families it into a cell the book still orders instead of un-writing it, and `refamilied` above is the whole of what that changed.

persons.name: Samuel Stout
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'samuel stout' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 32, reprinted over 3 consecutive issues — dated 1834-07-02 to 1834-07-16. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

citations.citation: "Early Chicago Voter Lists" — the poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago (10 August 1833), the tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833, the election returns and poll list of 1834 filed 11 August 1834, and the 1835 poll list. Transcribed from the Illinois Regional Archives Depository originals by Ingrid Latimer Schulz, published in Chicago Genealogist XXV/4 (Summer 1993), and republished by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team.

transcribes.work: Poll list for the first election of Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago (10 August 1833)
transcribes.note: 30 entries. Andreas says twenty-eight men voted at this election; the list prints thirty names. T-0542 searched for a count outside Andreas and found none — the Chicago Democrat did not exist until 26 November 1833 and its whole run to August 1835 carries no retrospective count of this poll — so the discrepancy STANDS, with the negative search recorded (claims/town_findings_voter_lists.json v004). On weight the thirty are the enrolments and Andreas's twenty-eight is an 1884 belief-statement ('It is believed') about the number of legal voters; neither count is repaired.

transcribes.work: Tax List of the Town of Chicago - 1833
transcribes.note: 115 entries. Names only — as published it carries no valuation, no lot and no figure, so it is not a ranked property roll (claims/town_findings_voter_lists.json v001).

transcribes.work: Election Returns - Poll List of 1834, filed 11 August 1834
transcribes.note: 115 entries. Andreas independently dates the second town election to 11 August 1834, which corroborates the list's own heading.

85 entries. THE LIST PRINTS NO DATE, AND IT IS NOT THE POLL BOOK OF THE THIRD TOWN ELECTION. That election is now dated from the town's own newspaper rather than from Andreas: the Chicago Democrat of 8 July 1835 announced the election of Trustees under the new charter for 'Friday of this week' and the issue of 15 July reported that it 'took place on Friday last' with the return — FRIDAY 10 JULY 1835, nine days after the 1835-07-01 scene date (claims/town_election_1835_democrat.json d001-d005). Andreas's town chapter, 'in July, 1835', is corroborated; his police chapter's 5 August 1835 is the day the newly elected board sat and passed the town's ordinance code over Hugunin's name as President. But that return gives single candidates 124 and 142 votes, which 85 men cannot cast, and six of the ten men who stood are absent from these 85 while the list runs unbroken from Adams to Wright — so this is a DIFFERENT poll, not a short printing of that one (claims/town_findings_voter_lists.json v003). Which poll is open; the county and state general election of Monday 3 August 1835 is the nearest candidate. Until it is settled, a name here evidences presence in Chicago in 1835 and not presence on any particular day.

what_it_supplies: 345 names of men who voted at, or were taxed by, the Town of Chicago in 1833, 1834 and 1835, as printed
which of the four lists each name stands on, and its position in that list
the courtesy and rank titles the lists print in front of a name (Col., Lt., Major, Dr.)

for the 1835 poll list: presence in Chicago during 1835, which is the strongest residence evidence this project holds short of a newspaper naming the man — but NOT presence on a stated day, because the list is undated and is shown not to be the poll book of the 10 July 1835 town election (T-0542)
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, street, lot or dwelling
any age, trade, household or family member
any date more precise than a list's own heading — and the 1835 list has no heading date at all
any woman, and any man who neither voted nor was taxed
